claims.text: Larger atomic size mismatches enhance atomic-scale lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
The proposed starting materials are homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys with solid-solution microstructures and minimal secondary phases.
Atomic size mismatch will be varied while overall composition and processing conditions are held constant.
Comparisons will be performed at room temperature under quasi-static loading using alloys with similar grain size, single-phase structures, and identical processing.
Increasing atomic size mismatch intensifies local lattice distortion.
More intense local lattice distortion raises the barrier to dislocation nucleation.
More intense local lattice distortion raises the barrier to dislocation glide.
Raising barriers to dislocation nucleation and glide enhances hardness.
Raising barriers to dislocation nucleation and glide enhances yield strength.
Alloys with larger atomic size mismatch will have higher hardness than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
Alloys with larger atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than the minimal-mismatch baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase high-entropy alloys under quasi-static room-temperature conditions.
Significant phase separation, ordering, or high-temperature recovery may invalidate the proposed relationship.
Short-range chemical ordering and local compositional variation may affect the quantitative relationship between atomic size mismatch and mechanical properties.
X-ray diffraction and TEM measurements can be used to quantitatively assess the relevant lattice distortions.
Failure of increased-mismatch samples to show both increased lattice distortion and enhanced hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposal requires atomic size mismatch to vary while overall composition remains constant. Because the mismatch is determined by constituent identities and their fractions, this is not operationally coherent unless 'overall composition' means only a broader constraint such as constant equiatomic ratios while element identities change; that clarification is absent.
